chunks.text: For basic night-sky photography, the NPS article lists a digital camera with manual controls, a wide-angle lens and a sturdy tripod. It recommends manual shooting mode. Long exposures collect light in dark scenes. This is general advice, not a Canon EOS R1-specific procedure.

NPS suggests opening the lens as wide as it allows, mentioning f/1.4 to f/3.5; beginning at ISO 400 and increasing as needed; and experimenting with exposures of 10 to 20 seconds. These are experimental starting settings in the article's tripod-based night-sky context, not guaranteed settings for every lens or a Canon EOS R1. Longer exposures can produce star trails as Earth rotates. The article does not provide an R1-specific maximum exposure time.

chunks.section: Set Up (white balance, release and focus)
chunks.text: NPS suggests automatic white balance and a two-to-five-second self-timer, a remote release, or a compatible smartphone. With camera and tripod positioned, manually focus using a distant bright light, such as a star, streetlight or house. These are general techniques; the article does not identify Canon EOS R1 menu paths or prove compatibility with a particular remote.

chunks.text: The NPS beginner guide suggests using the rule of thirds, surrounding objects as a frame, and leading lines to draw attention to the subject in outdoor photographs.
For a smoother moving-water effect, the guide suggests a slower shutter speed and keeping the camera steady, preferably on a tripod. It gives no universal waterfall exposure time.

The guide explains that a larger lens opening has a lower f-number, admits more light and gives shallower depth of field. A higher f-number can make the background clearer. These are general relationships, not guaranteed landscape sharpness or an EOS R1 setting recipe.
The guide describes shortly after sunrise or before sunset as golden hour, when sunlight has a warmer appearance and softer lighting.
